# Fast Approximation Algorithms for Balanced Edge and Vertex Separators

**Abstract**

We present a family of fast pseudo-approximation algorithms for the minimum balanced element cut problem in a graph, which includes vertex and edge separators. Given a graph _G_=(_V,E_) with polynomially-bounded finite integer element weights with _n_ vertices and _m_ edges, and a (constant) balance parameter \(c\in(0,1/2)\), where _G_ has some (unknown) _c_- balanced element cut of size OPT_<sub>c</sub>_, we give a (Monte-Carlo randomized) algorithm running in \(O(n^\varepsilon m^{1+o(1)})\) time that produces a \(\Theta(1)\)-balanced element cut of size \(O(OPT_c\cdot\sqrt{(logn)/\varepsilon})\) for any value \(\varepsilon\in[\Theta(1/log(n)),\Theta(1)]\). In particular, for any function \(f(n)=\omega(1)\) (including _f(n_)=loglog_n_, for instance), we can produce an element cut of size \(O(OPT_c\cdot\sqrt{logn}\cdot f(n))\) in time _O(m_<sup>1+_o_(1)</sup>). Moreover, for an arbitrarily small constant \(\varepsilon=\Theta(1)\), our algorithm also achieves the best-known approximation ratio for the vertex-separator specialization in \(O(m^{1+\varepsilon})\) time.

Our algorithms are based on a semidefinite programming (SDP) relaxation of the problem. A standard approach to solving an SDP relaxation for this kind of problem would use the primal- dual Matrix Multiplicative Weights Update framework of Arora and Kale, but this framework does not seem to apply, since we cannot express all of our SDPs primal variables explicitly. Instead, we present a new MMWU framework for our problem that allows us to represent some of our variables implicitly. We also extend our framework to a general **Partial-variable MMWU framework**, which we expect will be useful for future work. Our oracle for the balanced element cut problem within our framework uses \(O(n^\varepsilon\text{polylog}(n))\) almost-linear time maximum-flow computations, and would be sped up if the time complexity of maximum-flow improves.

For graphs with _padding bound_ \(\beta\), another oracle gives an \(O(\sqrt{\beta}/\varepsilon)\) approximation in \(m^{1+o(1)}n^\varepsilon\text{polylog}(n)\) time. It is known that \(\beta\le O(logh)\) for _K<sub>h</sub>_-minor-free graphs (and in particular \(\beta\le O(logn)\)).

### 1 Introduction

Partitioning a graph into smaller pieces is a fundamental problem that arises in many fields. One kind of graph partition with widespread applications in algorithms is the **vertex separator**: A small set of vertices whose removal disconnects the graph into small components.

More generally, let _G_=(_V,E_) be a graph with _n_=|_V_| vertices, let \(w:V\cup E\rightarrow\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}\) assign a polynomially-bounded weight to each vertex and edge, and let \(c\in(0,1/2)\) be a constant. For \(Z\subseteq V\cup E\), write \(w(Z)=\sum_{z\in Z}w(z)\). We treat vertex and edge separators in a common framework. A _c_-balanced **element cut** is a partition \(V=A\sqcup B\sqcup C\) with \(max\{|A|,|B|\}\le(1-c)n\), of cost

\(cost(A,B,C)=w(C)+w(E(A,B)).\)

It deletes the vertices in _C_ and the edges between _A_ and _B_. We also use \(w(z)=\infty\) as notation for forbidding deletion of an element _z_. Vertex separators are the specialization \(w(e)=\infty\) for all \(e\in E\), and edge cuts are the specialization \(w(x)=\infty\) for all \(x\in V\) . Write OPT_<sub>c</sub>_ for the minimum finite cost of a _c_-balanced element cut, _w_max for the maximum finite element cost, and _W_ for the sum of all finite element costs. Balance always counts original vertices. For fixed sets to separate,

Small vertex separators are known to exist for many classes of graphs with uniform weights \(w(\cdot)=1\). Planar graphs are known to admit \(\frac{1}{3}\)-balanced vertex separators of size \(O(\sqrt{n})\) \[43, 33\], genus-_g_ graphs are known to admit \(\frac{1}{3}\)-balanced vertex separators of size \(O(\sqrt{gn})\) \[21\], and similar results are known for minor-free graphs \[22\], geometric graphs \[37, 42\], induced-minor-free graphs \[25\], and other classes \[36, 12\]. These small separators also have numerous applications. To name a few, they naturally allow devising divide and conquer algorithms, dynamic programming algorithms, subexponential algorithms for NP-hard problems on special graphs, and maximum matching algorithms \[39, 34, 25\].

Unfortunately, while optimal planar separators can be found in linear time, none of these other results correspond to particularly fast algorithms often requiring exponential time in a parameter. For genus-_g_ graphs, the best-known separator theorem requires a surface-map/rotation system \[21\], which takes time exponential in _g_ to compute \[38, 6\], meaning it cannot be used to compute separators for graphs with even a small genus of polylog(_n_) in polynomial time. In the case of minor-free graphs, the time complexity can be even worse: One of the best-known separator theorems \[22\] corresponds to an algorithm which uses time proportional to multiple tower functions in the size of the minor. At best, some of the constructions correspond to polynomial-time algorithms (with a large polynomial overhead), such as those of induced-minor-free graphs \[25\], but such results are typically conjectured to be significantly sub-optimal existential bounds for the classes to begin with. Due to the significant overhead of these algorithms, many direct applications of recursively-separable graphs assume some routine is provided that produces a separator, and the time complexity of the assumed routine is incorporated into their final result \[15, 26, 2, 16, 23, 17, 10, 32, 44\].

Even for cases where the graph class might admit a fast algorithm (such as planar graphs), such algorithms only apply to graphs within their respective classes. In most practical settings for graph partitioning, we do not have any special guarantees that the graph falls into a certain class, but a graph might still have a small separator without properly falling into a special class: For instance, road networks, which are known to admit _empirically_ good separators \[14\], are _almost_ planar, in the sense that removing a relatively small number of vertices corresponding to structures like bridges will make them planar. Or, more theoretically, a graph could be nearly minor-free, in the sense that it contains a very large minor-free induced subgraph.

Thus, we naturally turn to the question of approximation algorithms: Given a graph _G_, can we approximate the minimum _c_-balanced vertex separator? It turns out that this is essentially impossible as-stated: It is NP-hard to approximate the minimum _c_-balanced vertex separator up to an _additive_ approximation of \(O(n^{\frac{1}{2}-\epsilon})\) for any \(\epsilon>0\) \[7\]. Fortunately, we may instead use _pseudo_-approximations (also called bi-criteria approximations): For a graph _G_ whose minimum _c_-balanced vertex separator has size OPT_<sub>c</sub>_, we can produce a \(\Theta(c)\)-balanced vertex separator with size close to OPT_<sub>c</sub>_.

Our first result is the following fast pseudo-approximation algorithm for finding a minimum balanced element cut. (When stating complexities, we always assume that \(m=\Omega(n)\) to simplify expressions; if it is not the case, then _m_ would need to be replaced with _m+n_).

**Theorem 1.** _For any_ \(\varepsilon\in[\Theta(1/logn),\Theta(1)]\) _and any constant_ \(c\in(0,1/2)\)_, there is a Monte-Carlo randomized algorithm (succeeding w.h.p.) that, given a graph G_=(_V,E_) _and polynomially-bounded finite integer element weights w, finds a_ \(\Theta(1)\)_-balanced element cut of size at most_ \(O(\mathrm{OPT}_c\cdot\sqrt{(\mathrm{log}n)/\varepsilon})\)_, where_ OPT_<sub>c</sub> is the minimum size of a c-balanced element cut. The algorithm runs in time_ \(O\left(n^\varepsilon\cdot T_\mathrm{maxflow}(m,m)\cdot\mathrm{polylog}(n)\right)\)_, where T_<sub>maxflow</sub>(_N,M_) _is the time to solve a max-flow problem on a graph with N vertices and M edges with capacities all_ poly(_n)._

By applying the almost-linear time maximum flow algorithm of Chen, Kyng, Liu, Peng, Gutenberg, and Sachdeva \[9\], we know that _T_<sub>maxflow</sub>=_O(m_<sup>1+_o_(1)</sup>). Specific choices of \(\varepsilon\) lead to the<tbc>

<tbc>following conclusions.

• Taking any fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), we obtain \(O(\sqrt{logn})\)-approximation in \(O(m^{1+\varepsilon})\) time. This approximation factor is the best known for both vertex- and edge balanced separators.<tbc>

• Taking \(\varepsilon=\Theta(1/logn)\), we obtain an _O_(log_n_)-approximation in \(O(T_{maxflow}(m,m)\cdot\text{polylog}(n))\) time. This will be useful if _T_<sub>maxflow</sub>(_m,m_) is ever improved to be near-linear.

## 1.1 Padding bound

**Definition 2.** _Graph_ (_V,E_) _has padding bound_ \(\beta\ge 1\) _if, for every nonnegative edge length vector_ \(\xi\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}^E\) _and every D\>_0_, the shortest-path pseudometric_ \(d(\cdot,\cdot)\) _with edge lengths_ \(\xi_{xy}\) _admits a distribution of partitions into sets of diameter at most D such that_

\(\mathtt{Pr}\left[B(x,\Gamma D)\subseteq P(x)\right]\ge e^{-\Gamma\beta}(x\in V)\)

_where_ \(B(x,r)=\{y\in V:d(y,x)\le r\}\) _is the ball of radius r centered at x, and P(x_) _is the part containing x. Here_ \(\Gamma>0\) _is a fixed absolute constant. We write_ \(\beta(G)\) _for the smallest padding bound of G_=(_V,E)._

_If we restrict to the case of edge length vectors_ \(\xi\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}^E\) _arising from vertex lengths_ \(\xi_v\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}^V\) _(so_ \(\xi_{uv}=\frac{1}{2}\xi_u+\frac{1}{2}\xi_v\)_), we obtain an analogous quantity we call_ \(\beta_v(G)\).

Many existing results are known for these padding bounds. Most are implied by the following results.

**Theorem 3** (Conroy-Filtser \[11\], Theorem 2)**.** _Every K<sub>h</sub>-minor-free graph G has_ \(\beta(G)\in O(logh)\).

**Theorem 4** (\[13, Theorem 1.4\])**.** _Every string graph G has_ \(\beta_v(G)\in O(1)\).

We will prove the following algorithmic result in terms of the padding bound.

**Theorem 5.** _For any_ \(\varepsilon\in[\Theta(1/logn),\Theta(1)]\) _and any constant_ \(c\in(0,1/2)\)_, there is a Monte-Carlo randomized algorithm (succeeding w.h.p.) that, given a graph G_=(_V,E_) _with padding bound_ \(\beta\) _(or with_ \(\beta_v(G)\le\beta\) _in the special case of vertex separators) and polynomially-bounded finite integer element weights w, finds a_ \(\Theta(1)\)_-balanced element cut of size at most_ \(O(OPT_c\cdot\sqrt{\beta}/\varepsilon)\)_, where_ OPT_<sub>c</sub> is the minimum size of a c-balanced element cut. The algorithm runs in time_ \(m^{1+o(1)}n^\varepsilon\text{polylog}(n)\)_. For fixed_ \(\varepsilon>0\)_, this is_ \(O(m^{1+\varepsilon})\).

In particular, by taking any fixed \(\varepsilon>0\) we obtain an \(O(\sqrt{\beta})\) approximation in \(O(m^{1+\varepsilon})\) time.

For comparison, when the partitions in Theorem 2 can be sampled efficiently, a standard polynomial-time LP-based approach \[31\] gives a \(O(\beta)\)-approximation (e.g., a _O_(log_h_)-approximation for _K<sub>h</sub>_-minor-free graphs \[11\]). Theorem 5 improves this to \(O(\sqrt{\beta})\). Moreover, it does not require that the partitions can be sampled efficiently. See table 1 for the direct applications to various graph classes.

## 1.2 History

Approximation algorithms for balanced vertex separators have a long history. First, it should be noted that there is a standard reduction from the balanced vertex separator problem to the (weighted) balanced directed edge separator problem based on vertex-splitting, preserving approximation ratios up to constants. For papers that study balanced directed edge separators directly, we will only discuss their implications for vertex separators.

Polynomial-time _O_(log_n_)-approximations date back to Leighton and Rao in 1988 \[30, 31\], and the best-known polynomial-time approximation ratio is \(O(\sqrt{logn})\), achieved independently by two groups at S 2005 \[18, 1\]. However, all of these algorithms are quite slow. The first requires up to _O(n_) solves of linear programs with a large number of constraints, while the latter two require up to _O(n_) solves of large semidefinite programs with a large number of constraints. The number of solves is because each problem is solving the related problem of _minimum-ratio vertex cut_: Roughly speaking, this refers to finding a set of vertices _S_ whose removal disconnects a small component _C_ of the graph, while minimizing |_S|/|C_|.

Progress on fast approximation algorithms with polylogarithmic approximation ratios has been much slower, and often involves unusual tradeoffs. In 2007, Arora and Kale presented an _O_(log_n_)- approximation using \(\widetilde{O}(1)\) strongly-polynomial maximum flow computations \[3\], and hence runs in \(\widetilde{O}(m^{1.5})\) time for a graph with _m_ edges. It should be noted that their algorithm does very much require strongly-polynomial maximum-flow, and does not admit an immediate replacement: The bit-complexity of the inputs to their flow problem is polylogarithmic _only_ if they are represented with floating point arithmetic. This prevents an immediate application of almost-linear time maximum flow \[9\], which applies for integer inputs of polynomial magnitude. That said, we think it is feasible that a slightly-modified form of their algorithm could be made to appropriately handle bit-complexity. This would require more work. Arora and Kale also presented an \(O(\sqrt{logn})\)- approximation running in \(\widetilde{O}(n^2+m^{1.5})\) time using multicommodity flow.

Since then, there have been a number of alternative results. In 2010, Louis \[35\] posted a preprint claiming to attain a polylogarithmic approximation in a polylogarithmic number of maximum flow computations using a "cut-matching game". Unfortunately, the details of this proof were never published. However, if the suggested algorithm does work, it does at least appear that it would not require any extra care for handling bit-complexity.

In 2019, Brandt and Wattenhofer \[5\] presented an algorithm with an alternative approximation guarantee: For a graph admitting a balanced 2/3-separator of size OPT, their algorithm produces a separator of size \(\widetilde{O}(OPT^2)\) in time \(\widetilde{O}(OPT^3m)\). This is useful for graphs with particularly small separators.

In 2024, Lau, Tung, and Wang \[28\] published a result implying a \(O(\sqrt{logn/\varepsilon})\)-approximation for the "vertex expansion" problem in \(O(n^{O(\varepsilon)})\) maximum flow computations, for a parameter \(\varepsilon\) similar to ours. This consequently implies a \(O(\sqrt{logn/\varepsilon})\)-approximation for the balanced vertex separators in \(O(n^{1+O(\varepsilon)})\) maximum flow computations via a standard reduction \[18\]. Unfortunately, their analysis omits consideration of bit-complexity, and so faces the same issue as Arora and Kale’s work (although it is again likely possible to handle with a more careful derivation).

## 1.3 Technical Overview

The overall structure of our algorithm is closest to the methods of Arora and Kale and follow-up works \[3, 40, 24\] for the balanced (edge) separator problem. Accordingly, we first give a brief overview of the latter problem, and discuss the precise point at which the same approach fails, requiring new ideas. Our method also bears some similarities to a slightly different approach of Lau, Tung, and Wang \[28\] for the directed edge expansion problem, and we discuss where this approach fails as well. Both of these previous works, as well as ours, make use of the "Matrix Multiplicative Weights Update" algorithm (MMWU), which is an online learning algorithm for the so-called "Matrix game" \[3, Algorithm 1\]. However, their implementations of this algorithm differ significantly.

### Balanced edge separator

First, the methods of Arora and Kale define an SDP relaxation of the problem that involves vector-valued variables \(v_i\in\mathbb{R}^n\) for each node \(i\in V\) . This relaxation is then approximately solved using a primal-dual Matrix Multiplicative Weights Update **framework** \[3, Algorithm 2\] (called the "Primal-Dual Algorithm for SDPs" in the cited version of their work), which internally runs the MMWU algorithm while maintaining the variables _v<sub>i</sub> explicitly_. The main subroutine of the primal-dual MMWU framework is a procedure called Oracle that does the following: given the current primal solution (i.e. vectors _v<sub>i</sub>_), it either finds a balanced separator of small cost, or finds an inequality violated by this solution (specified by dual variables). This inequality is then used to update vectors _v<sub>i</sub>_. This pair of valid outputs is key to keeping the "width" low, which in turn allows for a fast time complexity.

Different implementations of the oracle are presented in \[3\], \[40\] and in \[24\]. In particular, the oracle in \[24\] works by running a sequence of maximum flow computations, extracting directed matchings from these computations (via flow decompositions), and then "chaining" together these matchings.

### Sparse directed edge cuts

Lau, Tung, and Wang take an alternative approach to integrating the MMWU algorithm into their problem. There is a natural SDP relaxation of their problem as well, but it would naturally involve both a vector-valued variable \(v_i\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and a separate real- valued variable \(r_i\in\mathbb{R}\) for each node \(i\in V\) , with surprisingly challenging inequalities relating these two (see also \[27\] for related SDPs with similar structure). The standard primal-dual MMWU framework has no way to handle this structure, so Lau, Tung, and Wang instead use a min-max form of their problem, with outer vector-valued variables \(v_i\in\mathbb{R}^n\). In their case, the constraints on the vector-valued variables in this min-max form happen to coincide with precisely the guarantees that are maintained by the MMWU algorithm at all times. They then construct another Oracle procedure that either solves the inner problem in a way that has low "width", or outputs a combinatorial solution.

Importantly, their approach to analysis is rather ad-hoc, and only seems applicable to their specific problem, while making constraints like balance much more difficult to handle nicely.

On the technical level, our work introduces two new ideas, which are described below.

### Technical contribution #1: partial variable MMWU framework

For simplicity, let us consider vertex separators. We start by defining an SDP relaxation of the problem which is a variant of the SDP for the balanced edge separator (and distinct from previous SDP relaxations for balanced vertex separators such as the SDP of Feige-Hajiaghayi-Lee \[18\]). Besides variables<tbc>

<tbc>\(v_i\in\mathbb{R}^n\), we use scalar variables \(x_i\ge 0\) that indicate whether node _i_ belongs to the separator.

One could now try to apply the primal-dual MMWU framework described above: maintain primal variables _v<sub>i</sub>,x<sub>i</sub>_, find an inequality violated by these variables, and update these variables. Unfortunately, we were unable to find such a scheme. Variables _v<sub>i</sub>_ and _x<sub>i</sub>_ play very different roles, and it is not clear how to jointly update them while having a small "width" of the oracle. We also tried to find a usable min-max formulation, but, as mentioned, the balance requirement prevents the same trick of [28] from being applied to our problem, since the MMWU algorithm does not automatically satisfy these constraints.

Overcoming this difficulty was the first technical challenge that we faced. To resolve it, we avoid the standard primal-dual MMWU framework, and instead use a hybrid of the two approaches (which we will call the "partial-variable" MMWU framework): we maintain and update variables _v<sub>i</sub>_, but not _x<sub>i</sub>_. The latter are maintained neither explicitly nor implicitly, even though they are part of the primal SDP formulation. We carefully design an oracle that does not need variables _x<sub>i</sub>_ as input, while still outputting dual variables, and we apply the MMWU regret-minimization bound directly to the output of this oracle. We also extend this framework to a more general class of SDPs.

**Technical contribution #2: new oracle for the padding bound** To prove Theorems 1 and 5, we provide two different implementations of the oracle. The oracle for the first theorem is very close to the one in [24]; the main difference is that we generalize the minimum _s-t_ cut subroutine for edge separator to _element_ separators. For Theorem 5 we use a very different approach. First, we use random sampling to construct an instance of a multicommodity flow problem, which we then approximately solve using the algorithm in [8]. If the flow is large then its demand graph gives a valid output of the oracle (a feedback matrix of small width). The case of small flow is the most technically challenging part of the analysis. First, we use dual prices of the multicommodity flow problem to construct a shortest path pseudometric on _V_ . We then apply the definition of the padding bound and show the existence of Lipschitz approximation to Gaussian projections. Using this approximation, we finally prove that an _s-t_ minimum cut computation for a random Gaussian direction yields a balanced element cut of small cost with constant probability.

## 1.3.1 Bit complexity

Like previous works [3, 28], we apply maximum flow as an important subroutine. Moreover, depending on the value of the maximum flow, we may need to produce a corresponding minimum cut. For both vertex capacitated and directed graphs, the fastest-known maximum flow algorithm (exact, approximate, or otherwise) is the recent almost-linear time exact maximum flow result of Chen et al. [9], which only applies to networks with bounded integral capacities. This presents an issue for prior work: As presented, both the work of Arora and Kale for balanced edge separator [3] and its follow-up works [40, 24], as well as the work of Lau, Tung, and Wang [28] present their algorithms for real-valued weights. Since almost-linear time maximum flow requires bounded integers, a bit more work would be required to complete the analysis in these works in this paradigm.

In the case of balanced edge separator, there are alternative strongly near-linear-time undirected maximum flow routines that may be used instead [20]. However, in the case of directed edge expansion, there is no such alternative.

For our problem, we use the element-capacitated network to devise our maximum flow instances in such a manner that their capacities do not depend on the maintained variables {_v<sub>i</sub>_} in any way. However, while this is the main step required to avoid such issues, this does not automatically handle our bit complexity bounds, since our capacities do still depend on a number of different quantities, including our finite element costs, a guess at the value of the optimum solution (obtained via binary search), and several constants. To handle this cleanly, we parametrize some of our maximum flow instance capacities with a parameter \(\mu\), and prove several intermediate results for<tbc>

a value of \(\mu\) falling into a wide range. Then, our final proofs pick an appropriate value of \(\mu\) that falls into that range while having small bit-complexity.

## 2 Preliminaries

We will now define the main convex relaxation we will work with. Let \(\xi:=\frac{9}{4}c^2\), let \(\mathcal{S}:=\{S\subseteq V:|S|\ge\left(1-\frac{c}{4}\right)n\}\), and let P be the set of sequences \(p=(p_0,\dots,p_{\ell(p)})\) of distinct nodes in _G_. We use the notation \(p=(p_0,\dots,p_{\ell(p)})\) for the sequence of vertices along a path \(p\in\mathcal{P}\). (We write _ij_ for an undirected edge with endpoints _i,j_.) We consider the following relaxation of the _c_-balanced element cut problem:

The left and right sides here both denote the same optimization problem. The difference is notational. We have _L<sub>ij</sub>_=L(_G_<sub>(_i,j_)</sub>) and _T<sub>p</sub>_=L(_G<sub>p</sub>_)-L(\(G_{(p_0,p_{\ell(p)})}\)) where \(\mathcal{L}(\cdot)\) is the Laplacian of the corresponding graph (the diagonal degree matrix minus the adjacency matrix) and _G<sub>q</sub>_ for a path _q_ is the undirected unweighted graph containing all edges of _q_. Finally, we define _K<sub>S</sub>(i,i_)=|_S_|-1 for \(i\in S\), _K<sub>S</sub>(i,j_)=-1 for distinct \(i,j\in S\), and _K<sub>S</sub>(i,j_)=0 in all other cases.

In this section we assume that \(\beta(G)\le\beta\), or that \(w(e)=\infty\) for all \(e\in E\) and \(\beta_v(G)\le\beta\) (see Definition 2).

We start with some definitions. A set \(Q=A\times B\), where \(A,B\subseteq S\) are disjoint, is a _rectangle_. We denote \(\langle Q\rangle=\{\{x,y\}:(x,y)\in(A\times B)\cup(B\times A)\}\subseteq\genfrac(){pt}{2}{S}{2}\). Let _Q_<sup>paths</sup> consist of the simple graph paths _p_ with \(\partial p\in\langle Q\rangle\). For a set Q={_Q_<sub>1</sub>_,...,Q<sub>q</sub>_} with _q_=|Q| rectangles define \(\langle\mathcal{Q}\rangle=\bigcup_i\langle Q_i\rangle\subseteq\genfrac(){pt}{2}{S}{2}\) and \(\mathcal{Q}^\mathtt{paths}=\bigcup_iQ_i^\mathtt{paths}\).

**Definition 14.** _A set_ Q _is a_ \((\varepsilon,\Delta)\)-rectangular cover _if every pair_ \(\{x,y\}\in\langle\mathcal{Q}\rangle\) _satisfies_ \(\|x-y\|^2\ge\varepsilon\)_, and every pair_ \(\{x,y\}\in\genfrac(){pt}{2}{S}{2}\) _with_ \(\|x-y\|^2\ge\Delta\) _belongs to_ \(\langle\mathcal{Q}\rangle\)_. \(\sum_{p:x\in p}\nu(p)\le w(x)/2(x\in V)\) (7a)

\(\sum_{p:e\in p}\nu(p)\le w(e)(e\in E)\) (7b)

\(\sum_{p:x\in\partial p}\nu(p)\le\mu(x\in S)\) (7c)

Our algorithm will work as follows. First, we will generate a set of rectangles Q by sampling Gaussian directions which w.h.p. will be an \((\varepsilon,\Delta)\)-rectangular cover for \(\Delta=\Theta(1)\) (Sec. 6.1). Next,<tbc>

## 6.2 Solving the maximum \(\mu\)-uniform Q-flow problem

We will reduce the problem to a maximum multicommodity flow problem in a directed weighted graph G and then apply the algorithm of Chen-Graur-Sidford \[8\] for the latter problem. Start with the network \(\mathcal{N}(\varnothing,\varnothing,\mu)\) of Section 5, remove _s,t_, and add:

• for each \(x\in S\), nodes \(x^\ominus,x^\oplus\), an arc \((x^\ominus,x^\oplus)\) of capacity \(\mu\), and infinite-capacity arcs \((x^\oplus,x^+)\) and \((x^-,x^\ominus)\);<tbc>

• for each rectangle \(Q_i=A_i\times B_i\), private nodes _s<sub>i</sub>,t<sub>i</sub>_ and infinite-capacity arcs \((s_i,x^\ominus)\) for \(x\in A_i\) and \((y^\oplus,t_i)\) for \(y\in B_i\).

Note that G has _M=O(mq_) nodes and edges.

Now consider the maximum multicommodity flow problem in G with _q_ terminal pairs \(\{(s_i,t_i)\}_{i=1}^q\). We claim that it is equivalent to the maximum \(\mu\)-uniform Q-flow problem, i.e. there are value- preserving transformations between the problems in each direction. Indeed, use the path lifting and projection from Lemma 12(b) for the vertex and edge gadgets. For a path with endpoints \(a\in A_i,b\in B_i\), prepend \((s_i,a^\ominus,a^\oplus)\) and append \((b^\ominus,b^\oplus,t_i)\). The gadget arcs enforce exactly the vertex and edge loads, and each endpoint gate is used once per incident demand, enforcing the shared bound \(\mu\) across all rectangles and both endpoint roles. Conversely, remove flow cycles and project each simple _s<sub>i</sub>-t<sub>i</sub>_ path. Such a path cannot traverse an endpoint gate internally, since it would revisit the corresponding split vertex; private sources and sinks cannot occur internally either. The resulting paths therefore lie in \(Q_i^\text{paths}\) and satisfy all three load constraints with the same total value.

Next, we apply the algorithm in \[8\] for the approximate multicommodity flow problem. It produces a flow of value at least \((1-\varepsilon')\) of the optimum in \(O(M^{1+o(1)}q/\varepsilon')\) time, assuming that weights are polynomially-bounded integers. (In our case edges with infinite weights can be safely replaced with _Mc_<sub>max</sub>+1 where _c_<sub>max</sub> is the maximum finite weight in G). Cycle removal and endpoint decomposition take _O(M_log(_n+q_)) time per commodity using dynamic trees \[41, Section 6\] and pseudo-decomposition \[40, Lemma 3.7\]. Recording only the endpoint pairs and their weights constructs the demand graph \(D_\nu\) with _O(Mq_) edges in total, without listing path interiors.

We arrive at the following result.

**Theorem 17.** _For a given value_ \(\mu=a/b\) _with polynomially-bounded integers a,b we can in m_<sup>1+_o_(1)</sup>_q_<sup>2+_o_(1)</sup> _time compute a_ \(\mu\)_-uniform_ Q_-flow_ \(\nu\)_, represented implicitly, of value at least_ OPT<sub>Q</sub>/2_, and construct the demand graph_ \(D_\nu\) _with O(mq_<sup>2</sup>) _edges._

**Remark 1.** _Alternatively, an approximate_ \(\mu\)_-uniform_ Q_-flow with desired guarantees could be computed via calls to a minimum-cost flow subroutine using the MWU framework; this was the solution originally proposed by AI. We replaced it with a reduction to the algorithm in \[8\], which is a shorter way to get the desired complexity._

## 7.1 Chaining algorithm

The remaining part is identical to the algorithm in \[24\]. Assume that case (i) in Lemma 23 holds (otherwise calling `Matching`(_u_) for _u_∼N(0_,I<sub>d</sub>_) will terminate the oracle after _O_(1) expected calls). Assume also that \(\mathtt{Matching}(\cdot)\) is _skew-symmetric_, i.e. `Matching`(-_u_) is obtained from `Matching`(_u_) by reversing edge orientations. (This can be easily enforced algorithmically). The idea is to use procedure \(\mathtt{Matching}(\cdot)\) to find many "violating paths", i.e. paths \(p=(p_0,\dots,p_{\ell(p)})\) that satisfy

\(\sum_{j=1}^{\ell(p)}\|p_j-p_{j-1}\|^2\le\|p_{\ell(p)}-p_0\|^2-\Delta\) (17)

\(M\circ M'=\{p\circ q:p\in M,q\in M',\mathtt{endpoint}(p)=\mathtt{startpoint}(q)\}\)
